Introduction
?

In previous lessons, we've seen how some sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication operations exhibit properties similar to

In this lesson, we will formally define what we mean by a vector space.

First, let be a set equipped with the following two operations:

Vector addition:

For any two elements there is a unique element that also lies in We say that is closed under vector addition.

Scalar multiplication:

For any element and any number there is a unique element that also lies in We say that is closed under scalar multiplication.

A set equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication forms a vector space if it satisfies the following vector space axioms.

Axioms of Vector Addition ()

  • : for any ; vector addition is commutative.

  • : for any ; vectors addition is associative.

  • : There exists a zero-vector such that .

  • : For every there exists such that ; is called the negative of .

Axioms of Scalar Multiplication ()

  • : for any ; multiplying by does not change a vector.

  • : for any numbers and any vector .

Axioms Connecting Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication (the Distributive Laws)

  • : for any numbers and any vector .

  • : for any number and any vectors .

So, a vector space is simply a collective term for all kinds of sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication, where these operations satisfy this particular list of axioms (which are similar to the properties of these operations in ).

The elements of any vector space are called vectors.

  • Addition of matrices is commutative. ✓

Let L be the set of all functions f:R→R of the form f(x)=ax+1, where a∈R. Complete the following sentence:

L is not a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication of a function by a real number) because _________.
multiplication of f∈L by a scalar is not closed
addition and scalar multiplication of functions in L do not satisfy the distributive laws
addition of functions in L is not commutative
addition of functions in L is not associative
1⋅f≠f for some f∈L
multiplication of f∈L by a scalar is not closed
addition and scalar multiplication of functions in L do not satisfy the distributive laws
addition of functions in L is not commutative
addition of functions in L is not associative
1⋅f≠f for some f∈L

The correct answer is as follows:

L is not a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication of a function by a real number) because multiplication of f∈L by a scalar is not closed.

For example, if α=2 and f(x)=x+1, then αf(x)=2x+2. So, αf(x)∉L because the constant term is not 1.

On the other hand:

  • Addition of real valued functions is associative. ✓

  • Addition of real valued functions is commutative. ✓

  • 1⋅f=f for all f∈L. ✓

  • Addition and scalar multiplication of real valued functions satisfy the distributive laws. ✓
